name: Mesotherapy

lead: Mesotherapy means injecting small amounts of vitamins, medications, hyaluronic acid or plant extracts into or just under the skin, aiming for fuller hair, fresher skin and less local fat. In looksmaxxing communities it comes up most for scalp treatment alongside hair-loss drugs.

It was developed in France in 1952 by Michel Pistor, initially for pain. Proponents say microinjections form a local depot giving higher local concentrations, and that the needle trauma itself stimulates repair. Small trials and reviews report benefit in some pain and hair-loss settings, while cosmetic uses have generally not been tested in standard trials and mixtures vary widely.

paras: A practitioner injects the chosen mixture through fine needles in a series of sessions, or uses a needle-free pressurised version. Ingredients differ by practitioner and goal, and for hair it is typically combined with other hair-loss treatments.

Reported harms include injection-site infections, allergic reactions, tissue damage and inflammation. Outbreaks of rapidly growing mycobacteria followed procedures in Brazil, and Australian clients developed abscesses. In the US practitioners are overseen by state boards; only deoxycholic acid (Kybella) is approved for submental fat, and some countries restrict cosmetic uses.

chain: Local effect on skin, hair or fat
Fuller hair, fresher skin, less fat
angle.text: Mesotherapy is used to micro-inject vitamin and drug cocktails for thicker-looking hair, rejuvenated skin and local fat reduction. The idea is a concentrated local effect in the scalp, skin or fat. Small studies cover some uses, such as scalp treatment, while mixtures vary widely.

lead: Mesotherapy, also called local intradermal therapy, is a technique in which small doses of drugs, vitamins, minerals, enzymes, hyaluronic acid or plant extracts are injected through fine needles into the dermis or just beneath the skin. Its stated aim is localised action with minimal systemic exposure.[1][2] A needle-free pressurised version delivers the ingredients with a jet of air.[2]

French physician Michel Pistor is credited with developing it in 1952, initially using procaine injections for pain and vascular disorders; the term mesotherapy dates to 1958 and the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a medical specialty in 1987.[1][2] Cosmetic uses developed later and include skin rejuvenation, hair loss and localised fat and cellulite treatment, and phosphatidylcholine injections for fat gained attention in Brazil and the United States.[3]

The scientific record is mixed. Small trials and reviews report benefit in some pain and hair-loss settings, while Wikipedia states that cosmetic uses have generally not been tested in standard clinical trials, and reviews cite small samples and unstandardised mixtures.[1][2][3] Infection outbreaks have followed non-sterile practice.[4][5] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly for hair loss alongside drug regimens.[6]
infobox: Skin rejuvenation, hair loss, localised fat
Technique not FDA-approved; Kybella approved for submental fat[2]

paras: The method uses multiple shallow injections, typically no deeper than a few millimetres, over or near the target area, with small volumes of drug mixtures chosen by the practitioner.[1] Pistor summarised the approach as small volume, few times, in the right place.[1] Ingredients reported across practitioners include vitamins, enzymes, hyaluronic acid, procaine, dutasteride-containing preparations and, in some clinics, platelet-rich plasma.[2][7][8]

Pistor first applied the technique to pain and vascular disorders in 1952; the French press coined the term in 1958, a French society was founded in 1964, and the Academie Nationale de Medecine recognised it in 1987.[1][2] It later spread through Europe, South America, Asia and the United States, notably for cosmetic fat reduction.[1][3] A 2006 review in Dermatologic Surgery sought to clarify the historical distinction between mesotherapy and phosphatidylcholine injections popularised in Brazil.[3] An Italian society published a consensus report on its definition and clinical role in 2011.[9]

A study of a dutasteride-containing mesotherapy preparation in female pattern hair loss reported photographic, morphometric and ultrastructural evaluations of response.[7] Grokipedia notes that systematic reviews as of 2024 describe promising results for hair loss but call for larger trials.[1] A registered retrospective study compared PRP with mesotherapy in androgenetic alopecia.[10]

Wikipedia reports that a 10-patient study of facial multivitamin mesotherapy found no clinically relevant rejuvenation, while proponents describe hydration and collagen stimulation from hyaluronic acid and other substances.[1][2] A laboratory study of activated PRP on human dermal fibroblasts, which notes PRP has been used clinically in mesotherapy for skin rejuvenation, examined effects on extracellular matrix remodelling.[8]

Wikipedia states that no conclusive research shows any compound specifically targets fat cells, and that any effect might result from the detergent-like cell lysis of deoxycholic acid; plastic surgeon Rod Rohrich is quoted as saying he knows of no data that mesotherapy works.[2] A histology study examined tissue changes after mesotherapy for fat dissolution.[11] The only well-supported product is deoxycholic acid (Kybella), approved by the FDA for submental fat on the basis of a phase III trial of about 2,600 patients.[2]

Grokipedia says randomised trials in musculoskeletal pain have shown reductions in pain and improved function.[1] Registered trials compare mesotherapy with other approaches in conditions such as lateral epicondylitis, knee osteoarthritis and chronic shoulder pain.[12][13][14]

Risks listed include infection, allergic reactions and tissue damage when procedures are non-sterile or done by unqualified practitioners.[1] An outbreak affecting 311 patients in Belem, Brazil, in 2004-2005 involved rapidly growing mycobacteria after laparoscopic surgery and other procedures, including eight patients who had mesotherapy.[4] A new Mycobacterium species was described from a cosmetic infection and a nail salon,[5] and Wikipedia mentions Australian reports of skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection.[2] A US dermatologist warned that phosphatidylcholine can cause unpredictable and severe inflammation.[2] In France a 2011 ban on mesotherapy for fat removal was lifted after investigators attributed problems to unhygienic practice rather than the method.[2]

Human studies include a dutasteride mesotherapy study in women with pattern hair loss,[7] a histology study of mesotherapy for fat dissolution,[11] and a prospective controlled study of PRP for collagen formation in skin rejuvenation.[15] Registered trials cover non-cosmetic uses such as lateral epicondylitis, knee osteoarthritis, myofascial pain and shoulder pain,[12][13][14][16] as well as facial scars with botulinum toxin and vitamin C mesotherapy for gingival pigmentation.[17][18] Grokipedia describes overall validation as limited by small samples, non-standard mixtures and few large randomised trials.[1]

In the United States the FDA cannot control what practitioners inject and state medical boards oversee the practice; the American Society of Plastic Surgeons has not endorsed mesotherapy and the American Society for Dermatologic Surgery has said further study is needed.[2] Several South American countries ban it, Brazil has prohibited it for fat uses, and Italy restricts it to licensed medical professionals.[1][2]

A looksmax.org thread describes a user told by a hair transplant clinic that scalp mesotherapy plus an oral and topical drug regimen could thicken his hairline without a transplant, and asks others whether it would work.[6] In forums the term is mostly attached to hair-loss protocols that combine mesotherapy with finasteride or dutasteride and minoxidil.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org mesotherapy appears chiefly as a scalp treatment discussed alongside hair-loss drugs.[6]

claims.claim: Scalp mesotherapy can regrow or thicken hair and may replace a transplant.
Mesotherapy cocktails dissolve fat or rejuvenate skin.
Mesotherapy is safe because it uses very small doses.

timeline.event: Michel Pistor develops mesotherapy using procaine injections for pain and vascular disorders.[1][2]
French Academy of Medicine recognises mesotherapy as a specialty.[1][2]
Mycobacterial outbreaks in Belem, Brazil begin, including mesotherapy patients.[4]
Italian Society of Mesotherapy consensus report; France lifts its ban on fat-removal mesotherapy.[2][9]
